verses.text: The burden of Damascus: “Behold, Damascus is taken away from being a city, and it will be a ruinous heap.
The cities of Aroer are forsaken. They will be for flocks, which shall lie down, and no one shall make them afraid.
The fortress shall cease from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus, and the remnant of Syria. They will be as the glory of the children of Israel,” says Yahweh of Armies.
“It will happen in that day that the glory of Jacob will be made thin, and the fatness of his flesh will become lean.
It will be like when the harvester gathers the wheat, and his arm reaps the grain. Yes, it will be like when one gleans grain in the valley of Rephaim.

Yet gleanings will be left there, like the shaking of an olive tree, two or three olives in the top of the uppermost bough, four or five in the outermost branches of a fruitful tree,” says Yahweh, the God of Israel.
In that day, people will look to their Maker, and their eyes will have respect for the Holy One of Israel.
They will not look to the altars, the work of their hands; neither shall they respect that which their fingers have made, either the Asherah poles, or the incense altars.
In that day, their strong cities will be like the forsaken places in the woods and on the mountain top, which were forsaken from before the children of Israel; and it will be a desolation.
For you have forgotten the God of your salvation, and have not remembered the rock of your strength. Therefore you plant pleasant plants, and set out foreign seedlings.
In the day of your planting, you hedge it in. In the morning, you make your seed blossom, but the harvest flees away in the day of grief and of desperate sorrow.
Ah, the uproar of many peoples, who roar like the roaring of the seas; and the rushing of nations, that rush like the rushing of mighty waters!

The nations will rush like the rushing of many waters: but he will rebuke them, and they will flee far off, and will be chased like the chaff of the mountains before the wind, and like the whirling dust before the storm.
At evening, behold, terror! Before the morning, they are no more. This is the portion of those who plunder us, and the lot of those who rob us.

footnotes.content: Damascus will become a ruin—Isaiah names the burden plainly. This is what happens when nations abandon the Lord for self-sufficiency; even great cities crumble to heaps. The Lord is not capricious; He is patient, but patient does not mean forgiving forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Aroer's cities empty, and the land given over to sheep instead of people. There's a strange mercy here—not annihilation, but emptiness. The earth itself is allowed to rest, and sheep graze where kingdoms once clashed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fortress, kingdom, throne—all three fall away. Syria and Ephraim both stripped down, left as mere remnants. Yet the Lord measures their humbling by Israel's own glory; both nations are leveled not to oblivion but to equality in need.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob's glory grows thin, his flesh becomes lean. The metaphor is intimate—the nation wastes away like a man in sorrow. Yet this thinning is also a stripping of self-reliance, a making of room for the Lord alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The reaper gathers grain in the Valley of Rephaim—a place of ancient giants and battles, now only a field for harvest. Even destruction follows the orderly rhythm of God's hand, as deliberate as a harvester's sickle.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After the reaping comes the gleaning—two or three olives high in the tree, four or five on the branches. Not zero. The Lord leaves remnants, small and scattered, but real. He preserves a seed, always.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In that day, people will look to their Maker. Suffering turns the eye homeward. After the falling-away of cities and thrones, the human heart finally seeks what it should have sought always—the living God, not human handiwork.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No respect for altars, Asherah poles, or incense altars—the hand-carved gods of wood and stone. The Lord is saying: those things you made cannot be looked to; they will be forsaken as they are forsaken. Only He remains.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Strong cities become like abandoned places in woods and mountains, the ghost-towns of an earlier age. What once stood proud is swallowed back into wilderness—a quiet, steady reclamation by the earth itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You have forgotten the God of your salvation, the rock of your strength. Instead, you plant pleasant gardens and foreign seedlings—symbols of self-made security. The Lord names the heart's turning away plainly: you chose to forget Me for comfort.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You hedge, you sow, you make the seed blossom—such careful tending, yet the harvest flees in grief and sorrow. All the frantic labor of self-preservation comes to nothing. Only the Lord's planting bears fruit in the end.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The uproar of many peoples, roaring like the sea—nations rushing like mighty waters. The thunder of empires is real and terrifying. Yet Isaiah listens to the Lord speak above this noise, unafraid.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He will rebuke them; they will flee far off—chased like chaff in the wind, dust in the storm. The very nations that roar are scattered by a word. What seems so mighty to men is nothing before the Lord's rebuke.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At evening, terror; before morning, gone. The portion of those who plunder us is swift judgment. Readers today hear an echo: the Lord's peace comes not to those who trust in walls and weapons, but to those who trust in His morning—the assurance that He keeps watch while we sleep, and His justice needs no army.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
